name: Bia Hơi
description: Vietnam's fresh draught: brewed daily, delivered in kegs by moped, drunk on a plastic stool by the afternoon. Unpasteurised, barely carbonated, cheap as water.
funFact: Bia hơi has no shelf life at all — it is brewed, delivered and drunk within about 24 hours, which is why it exists only in Vietnam and why every street corner has its own supplier.

serve.how: Serve it very cold, and do not be alarmed when ice goes in the glass — that is the local custom and the beer is brewed light enough to take it. Pour into a plain glass with no expectation of head. Drink it the day it was made; there is no pasteurisation, no filtration and no attempt at stability, which is exactly the trade-off that makes it taste fresh.

composition.summary: An unpasteurised, low-strength draught lager brewed for immediate consumption.

components.label: Malt
components.detail: Barley malt cut generously with rice for lightness.

components.label: Hops
components.detail: Minimal — just enough to keep it from tasting flabby.

components.label: Yeast
components.detail: A fast lager strain, fermented and shipped within days.

components.label: Other
components.detail: No pasteurisation and no filtration, which is the defining choice.

composition.process: Fermented quickly, kegged unpasteurised and delivered the same day to be drunk before it can stale.

name: Happoshu
description: Japan's tax-engineered beer: deliberately brewed below the malt threshold that triggers the higher beer duty. A category invented by accountants and perfected by brewers.
funFact: Japanese liquor tax scales with malt content, so brewers reformulated below 67% malt to sell cheaper — the government kept lowering the bracket, and brewers kept reformulating, producing a genuine arms race in beer law.

serve.how: Serve very cold in a tall, narrow glass to hold what head there is. Pour with a bit of height to build foam, because the reduced malt gives a thinner body that benefits from the texture. It is engineered for refreshment rather than complexity, so drink it cold and fast alongside food rather than contemplating it.

composition.summary: A low-malt beer-like beverage formulated to sit under Japan's malt-based tax threshold.

components.label: Malt
components.detail: Under the legal malt threshold, supplemented with barley, corn or pea protein.

components.label: Hops
components.detail: Light, clean and restrained.

components.label: Yeast
components.detail: Standard Japanese lager yeast, fermented cold.

components.label: Other
components.detail: Adjuncts chosen as much for tax law as for flavour.

composition.process: Brewed as a lager but with the malt bill kept deliberately below the taxable percentage, then fermented cold and filtered bright.

name: Filipino Pale Pilsen
description: A deep-golden, all-malt pilsen with more bitterness than most tropical lagers dare — the Philippines' national beer since 1890 and still poured in stubby brown bottles.
funFact: San Miguel began brewing it in 1890 under a royal grant from Spain, making it the first brewery in Southeast Asia — the Philippine company later ended up owning the Spanish brand that named it.

serve.how: Serve cold from the bottle into a small glass, refilling often so it never warms — the Filipino habit of sharing one bottle around a table of small glasses exists for exactly that reason. Expect a firmer, drier bitterness than a typical tropical lager. It stands up to fried and vinegary food better than lighter lagers do.

composition.summary: An all-malt pale lager with assertive hopping, brewed in the Philippines since 1890.

components.label: Malt
components.detail: All barley malt, with no rice or corn adjunct.

components.label: Hops
components.detail: Noble-style hopping at a level that reads genuinely bitter.

components.label: Yeast
components.detail: Lager yeast fermented cool and conditioned.

components.label: Other
components.detail: Nothing — the absence of adjunct is the point of the style.

composition.process: A conventional cold lager fermentation, distinguished by an all-malt grist and a bitterness level unusual for the tropics.

name: Lion Stout
description: A full-strength tropical stout brewed at altitude in Sri Lanka and once dispensed from wooden casks in Kandy. Coffee, liquorice and dark fruit at eight percent.
funFact: Sri Lanka's stout tradition is a colonial inheritance that outlived its origin — Lion Stout was long served hand-pumped from wooden casks in hill-country pubs, a serving method Britain itself had largely abandoned.

serve.how: Serve cool rather than cold — at fridge temperature the coffee and dark fruit shut down completely. Pour into a snifter or a half-pint and give it ten minutes to open. At eight percent it is a sipping beer despite the tropical climate it was brewed for, and it takes sweet and spiced food better than it takes anything delicate.

composition.summary: A strong tropical stout built on roasted barley and dark crystal malt.

components.label: Malt
components.detail: Pale malt with roasted barley, chocolate and crystal malts.

components.label: Hops
components.detail: Enough to balance a heavy dark grist, no more.

components.label: Yeast
components.detail: Ale yeast fermented warm in a tropical climate.

components.label: Other
components.detail: Historically wooden cask conditioning, now largely bottled.

composition.process: Warm ale fermentation on a heavily roasted grist, conditioned to soften the roast into coffee and dried fruit.

name: Indian Strong Beer
description: India's dominant beer category: a high-strength lager built for maximum effect per rupee, sold in 650ml bottles and drunk very cold.
funFact: Strong beer accounts for the large majority of Indian beer sales — state excise structures and pricing make a 7–8% bottle better value than a 5% one, which is why the mild lagers barely sell.

serve.how: Serve extremely cold in a tall glass — this is a style that is helped rather than harmed by low temperature, since chilling mutes the alcohol and the sweetness. Pour into a chilled glass and refill from the large bottle as you go. Drink it with heavily spiced food, where its residual sweetness works as a counterweight to chilli heat.

composition.summary: A high-gravity pale lager brewed for strength, with adjuncts keeping the body drinkable.

components.label: Malt
components.detail: Barley malt with a large adjunct fraction of rice or maize.

components.label: Hops
components.detail: Low — bitterness is not the selling point.

components.label: Yeast
components.detail: Lager yeast pushed to a high final alcohol.

components.label: Other
components.detail: Adjuncts that raise strength without adding heaviness.

composition.process: A high-gravity cold fermentation with substantial adjunct, filtered bright and bottled at strength.

name: Chang
description: Himalayan grain beer of millet, barley or rice, fermented in a tub and drunk warm at altitude. Sour, cloudy and served with a wooden ladle.
funFact: At Himalayan altitude chang is drunk warm rather than cold, and often topped repeatedly with hot water from the same grain — the same practice as Nepali tongba, of which chang is the wider family.

serve.how: Serve warm rather than chilled — this is a cold-climate beer and refrigeration makes no sense at four thousand metres. Ladle it cloudy from the vessel, sediment and all. Expect a sour, bready ferment rather than anything crisp, and treat it as food as much as drink; it is calorie-dense by design.

composition.summary: A warm-served Himalayan grain beer fermented with a wild starter cake.

components.label: Malt
components.detail: Millet, barley or rice, cooked rather than malted in the European sense.

components.label: Hops
components.detail: None.

components.label: Yeast
components.detail: A dried starter cake carrying both yeast and mould cultures.

components.label: Other
components.detail: Hot water added repeatedly to the same grain bed.

composition.process: Cooked grain is inoculated with a starter cake, fermented for several days in a covered tub, then served warm and cloudy.

name: Chinese Rice Lager
description: The best-selling beer style on earth by volume, and almost nobody outside China thinks about it: pale, light-bodied, rice-heavy and brewed for drinking with food.
funFact: Snow, brewed in China, sells more volume than any other beer brand in the world — largely unknown outside the country because virtually all of it is drunk domestically.

serve.how: Serve cold in a small glass and refill often — Chinese table service pours small measures for repeated toasts rather than a single large glass. Expect very light body, low bitterness and a clean finish. It is engineered to sit under strongly flavoured food rather than compete with it, which is exactly what it does well.

composition.summary: A very light pale lager built on a large proportion of rice adjunct.

components.label: Malt
components.detail: Barley malt with a substantial rice fraction for lightness.

components.label: Hops
components.detail: Very low — bitterness is minimised deliberately.

components.label: Yeast
components.detail: Clean lager yeast, cold-fermented and filtered bright.

components.label: Other
components.detail: Rice, which thins the body and lightens the colour.

composition.process: Cold fermentation on a rice-heavy grist, filtered bright and pasteurised for a light, neutral beer.
